The Neretva chub (Squalius svallize) begins life as a small, yolk-dependent larva emerging from a demersal egg with a diameter of approximately 2.2 mm. Upon hatching, the prolarva carries a substantial yolk sac and weighs just 0.0056 grams [Wwb = 0.0056 grams], a remarkably modest starting mass that reflects the limited maternal provisioning typical of many small-bodied cyprinids. This lecithotrophic stage persists until the mouth opens and the larva commences exogenous feeding. During this early period, growth is heavily dependent on the absorption of yolk nutrients, and mortality is often elevated as the tiny fish must locate suitable planktonic prey. Field surveys of young-of-year in the Neretva River basin indicate that this initial phase is a critical bottleneck for recruitment. The transition to an actively feeding, free-swimming larva marks the onset of a rapid growth trajectory that continues through the summer months, during which the juvenile fish must accumulate sufficient energy reserves to survive the cooler winter period. The species is endemic to the Neretva River drainage in the western Balkans, where it occupies clear, well-oxygenated streams and karstic lakes, often in sympatry with other endemic cyprinids.

The onset of gonadal activity is triggered by a combination of rising spring water temperatures and increasing day length, with first spawning usually occurring during the months of April and May. The relatively small size at maturity suggests an opportunistic life-history strategy, enabling the species to begin reproductive activity early despite the risk of elevated predation on smaller adults. Age at first reproduction has been estimated at between one and two years for most individuals inhabiting the lower reaches of the river, although populations in cooler, higher-elevation streams may delay their first breeding event by an additional year. The short generation time is characteristic of many small-bodied leuciscids and allows the species to recover from population disturbances more rapidly than larger, longer-lived congeners.

As the Neretva chub continues to grow, it can ultimately achieve an asymptotic fork length of 27.7 cm [Li = 27.7 cm], though such large individuals are encountered relatively infrequently in the wild. Reaching this maximum recorded fork length corresponds to an ultimate wet body mass of approximately 245 grams [Wwi = approximately 245 grams], a value derived from length-weight relationships established for the species. Reaching this size requires several years of sustained growth, during which the fish must navigate the seasonal challenges of food availability, flow variation, and interspecific competition. Larger adults are typically found in the deeper pools and slower-flowing sections of the river, where they can more efficiently exploit benthic macroinvertebrate prey. Comparative data from related leuciscid species indicate that the asymptotic size of Squalius svallize is intermediate between that of smaller-bodied congeners such as Squalius tenellus and larger forms like Squalius cephalus. The capacity to reach this size is closely tied to the productivity of the karstic habitats the species inhabits, where calcium-rich waters support abundant populations of snails and insect larvae that form the bulk of the adult diet.

This estimate is based on detailed observations of a captive cohort held at the University of Mostar's ichthyology facility, where individuals were monitored until natural mortality occurred. In wild populations, maximum longevity may be somewhat shorter due to predation pressure and the energetic demands of seasonal reproduction. The relatively moderate lifespan of around seven years is consistent with the species' body size and life-history pace, placing it between short-lived annual cyprinids and longer-lived species such as common barbel (Barbus barbus), which can exceed fifteen years. The thermal regime of the Neretva River, which remains cool year-round due to karstic groundwater inputs, may contribute to a slightly extended lifespan compared to populations of the same species living in warmer, more variable lowland habitats. Senescence in this species is marked by a gradual decline in feeding activity and a loss of body condition during the final months of life.

The ultimate fork length of 27.7 cm [Li = 27.7 cm] and ultimate wet weight of 245 grams [Wwi = 245 grams] serve as benchmarks for trophy-size individuals in the recreational fishery, although such large fish are now rare due to habitat fragmentation and introduced predator species.
